newsitem.title: GERMANY: Missiles send German shares lower, but no selloff.
newsitem.headline: Missiles send German shares lower, but no selloff.

text.p: German shares dipped in nervous trading on Tuesday and could head still lower in coming sessions, but dealers did not expect U.S.-Iraqi tensions to trigger a massive selloff.
While dealers described the mood at twitchy and acknowledged that investors had sold German shares, they largely played down the impact of news that the U.S. had launched missile attacks on Iraq.
"I think no one will really be talking about this in a few days," one dealer said after the U.S. retaliated for weekend incursions by Iraqi troops into Kurdish areas.
The 30-share IBIS DAX index was down 1.12 percent at 2,509.85 points in late trading after closing floor trading at 2,510.77 points.
Compounding nervousness generated by rising political tensions, traders said a softer bond market and uncertainties about economic developments were also hurting the equities market.

One reason dealers expected political tensions to have little impact on trading for long was that the dollar, which is usually particularly sensitive to tensions like this, failed to react very strongly.
"Surely there is some selling pressure, but I just don't see the black clouds forming quite yet," added another dealer.
The index is supported at 2,500 and after that at 2,450, but dealers did not expect the market to fall that far in the near-term.
More interesting to the market are further clues on economic development, particularly after the U.S. National Association of Purchasing Managers index moved to 52.6 in August from 50.2 in July.
The numbers helped the share market curb some losses, particularly as the index showed a calm price sector.

Among individual German shares, Deutsche Bank remains under pressure after its Morgan Grenfell unit suspended dealing in three funds as regulators are investigating potential irregularities. Deutsche shares were down 52 pfennigs at 72.24 marks.

Similarly shares in national airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG dropped 3.94 percent to 200.05 marks as the group's chairman told a magazine that the group would seek a wage-freeze, hinting at a difficult business climate.
"Saying you need a wage freeze is pretty specific that the company is not doing that well," a dealer said.
